title: Doctor Vedika Magar Quit Her Government Job for Cricket — Now She Wants India's Jersey
excerpt: The Pandharpur MBBS graduate resigned a gazetted officer post, debuted for Sikkim in October 2026, and doubles as the Delhi Capitals women's team doctor while chasing an India cap.
body:
• Dr Vedika Magar, an MBBS graduate from Pandharpur, Maharashtra, resigned from a Class II gazetted officer post at a government hospital about a year ago to pursue professional cricket full-time.
  • After three years in Mumbai's domestic probables without a breakthrough, she made her professional debut for Sikkim against Kerala in the Senior Women's T20 Trophy in October 2026.
  • She has worked as team doctor for the Delhi Capitals women's team in the WPL since 2024, studying elite players including Meg Lanning and Shafali Verma from the dugout.
  • Her stated goals are explicit: "Every player playing cricket in India, including me, dreams of representing the country. My end goal is definitely to play for India."

Vedika Magar's career path reads like the plot of the 2024 film Mr. & Mrs. Mahi, in which a doctor gives up medicine to chase an India cricket jersey. Magar lived the non-fiction version. From Pandharpur, a town in Maharashtra where opportunities for women in cricket were limited, she studied medicine, secured a government job — and then, last year, resigned from it to pursue cricket professionally, she told India Today in an interview.

The choice her mentor forced

After securing admission to Grant Medical College and Sir JJ Group of Hospitals in Mumbai, Magar moved to the city for her MBBS but kept attending practice sessions and joined a coaching academy. Professor Dr Hemant Gupta, from the Department of Medicine, noticed her playing leather-ball cricket and began guiding her — then asked the question that changed her course: postgraduate studies, or professional cricket?

"Playing professional cricket had always been my childhood dream, but I had never imagined it would be possible. My internship was underway, I had a government job through my bond, and I had several other responsibilities. However, his guidance made me realise that I had to take a chance," she said. "I did not want to spend the rest of my life regretting that I had never tested my potential."

Four hours of sleep, and a fractured femur

The years of doing both were punishing. She practised two to three hours and then worked 12-hour shifts; in her first year she suffered a serious femur fracture, which she attributes largely to inadequate recovery. For almost a year she took night shifts — 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. — slept four to five hours, and practised in the afternoon. Few around her understood. "I was 23, had completed my MBBS and was working in a Class II gazetted officer-level position at a government hospital. So, when I decided to take up cricket professionally, people found it difficult to understand," she said. Her parents backed her: "If this is your passion and playing cricket makes you happy, go for it. Even if you don't reach the highest level, at least you won't regret never having tried."

"I resigned from my government job about a year ago. It was a good position, but I decided to leave it for cricket because I just couldn't manage both."

— Dr Vedika Magar

A debut, and a doctor's edge

Magar was named in Mumbai's domestic probables on three occasions, but the opportunity came from elsewhere: in October 2026 she made her professional debut for Sikkim against Kerala in the Senior Women's T20 Trophy. She has not left medicine entirely — since 2024 she has been associated with the Delhi Capitals set-up in the Women's Premier League as a team doctor, and she practises four to five hours a day under a senior doctor at a private clinic in Mumbai.

She argues the medical training accelerated her cricket. "From what I have observed, there is still a lack of awareness among female athletes, and athletes in general, at the grassroots level," she said, pointing to recovery, nutrition and strength training. Working alongside Meg Lanning, Jess Jonassen, Marizanne Kapp, Jemimah Rodrigues and Shafali Verma at Delhi Capitals, she studied how elite players train beyond skills — strength, power, recovery, nutrition and mental strength — and compressed those lessons into three to four years of catching up with competitors who had a decade's head start.

What she wants next

Magar plans to focus only on cricket for the next couple of years before deciding on postgraduate studies. The targets are named, not implied: a WPL playing contract, and India. "Every player playing cricket in India, including me, dreams of representing the country. My end goal is definitely to play for India. I want to wear that jersey. I also want to play in the WPL," she said. Read the full interview via The Net News.
